paras: The lynching of Claude Chandler took place on the night of August 29, 1920, when masked men took Chandler, a 19-year-old Black prisoner, from the Oklahoma County jail in Oklahoma City and hanged him west of the city. He was accused of killing two officers in a raid on his father's home near Arcadia. Governor J. B. A. Robertson charged that officers had colluded with the mob, and reports of armed Black men raised fears of a race riot.

On August 28 federal and county officers raided Charles Chandler's home near Arcadia, in Logan County, in search of an alleged moonshine still. Deputy Sheriff Homer Adrean, prohibition officer Stanton Weiss and Charles Chandler were killed in the shooting, and his son Claude was captured and accused of killing the officers. According to the Guthrie Daily Leader, Oklahoma County officers took him to Oklahoma City over Logan County officials' objections.

About 10 o'clock Sunday night one of the men gained entry to the jail by posing as an officer with a prisoner. The United Press reported that they overpowered jailer J. B. Saunders, cut the telephone wires and lights and carried Chandler off in automobiles. Wire reports counted 30 masked men, the Guthrie Daily Leader about 25, and the Tulsa Star only a few.

Next morning an unidentified caller told the sheriff where to find the body. It hung from a tree hidden by bushes near Council Grove, about eight miles west by the Associated Press count; other reports said six to ten miles. He had been shot in the head; the Black Dispatch reported two wounds in the forehead and his hands and feet tied.

Robertson ordered an investigation and wrote that the officers were either in collusion with the mob or unfit, urging removal of the sheriffs. The coroner's inquest was continued to Saturday, and assistant attorney general E. L. Fulton and County Attorney O. A. Cargill opened a closed-door inquiry. In September the attorney general's department asked the state supreme court to remove Sheriff G. E. Johnson, Saunders and a deputy for neglect of duty.

Reports of armed Black men driving in from Edmond and Arcadia led Cargill to arm deputies, and about 200 Black men gathered in the city. Officials later said the men in the cars were mostly relatives or friends coming to view the body, unarmed. Logan County claimed the body, which the Black Dispatch said was buried near Arcadia. On September 24 the Black Dispatch reported that the courthouse investigation had begun and predicted a whitewash; no report of an indictment appears in the coverage.

The wire story ran on August 30 and 31 from West Virginia to California and Montana, often under race-riot headlines such as the Memphis News Scimitar's "Armed Negroes Are Reported En Route To Oklahoma City." The Daily Ardmoreite called Chandler a "Black Bootlegger," and the Durant Weekly News mocked the killing under the headline "May Have Taken Him to Watermelon Feast." The Guthrie Daily Leader instead blamed Oklahoma County officers and said Chandler was not believed to have killed either officer.

Black papers took up the case on September 3 and 4. The Black Dispatch of Oklahoma City called it "the most dastardly and hellish crime" in the state and said the sheriff and jailer "had guilty knowledge of the act." The Tulsa Star wrote that he was lynched "largely because of his color." The Chicago Whip headed its brief "Lynched for Making Home Brew," and the Cleveland Advocate, naming him "Charles Chandler," wrote that "the lynchers go unmolested."

The two Oklahoma weeklies then quarreled. The Tulsa Star rebuked Black men who gathered after the lynching and let "one lone policeman" take their guns, while the Black Dispatch replied that about fifty white policemen had disarmed some six men in one car.

Most reports said Chandler was accused of killing the officers, but the Imperial Valley Press said bootlegging and the Chicago Whip resisting a search; the Guthrie and Tulsa papers doubted his guilt. Wire reports described unknown masked men, while the Guthrie Daily Leader alleged that Oklahoma County officers formed the mob, led by a deputy named Moore according to the Logan County sheriff.

reader.title: Lynching of Claude Chandler
bases: A band of masked men took Chandler, a Black prisoner accused of killing two officers, from the county jail at night and hanged and shot him outside the city (A2, A4, A26).

Chandler was killed by a party reported as 25 to 30 masked men who seized him from jail with no lawful authority (A1, A2, A7); he was held on an accusation of killing two officers and the Guthrie paper reported the crowd whispering of avenging them (A2, A7).

The United Press, the Associated Press, Oklahoma papers in Ardmore and Guthrie, and the Black Dispatch, which sent people to the scene, agree on the seizure from jail and the hanging (A1, A2, A7, A20, A26).

accounts.label: Wire report (UP/AP)
accounts.gist: About 30 masked men gained entry to the jail by a ruse, overpowered the jailer and took Chandler, accused of killing two officers; his body was found hanging west of the city.

accounts.label: Guthrie Daily Leader (Logan County)
accounts.gist: The mob was made up mainly of Oklahoma County officers and led by a deputy, the jailer was friendly with it, and Chandler was not believed to have killed either officer.

accounts.label: Jailer's account
accounts.gist: Men who said they were officers from another county with a prisoner overpowered and tied him and cut the lights and telephone wires.

accounts.label: Governor Robertson
accounts.gist: The jailer's excuse was too flimsy to believe; the officers were either in collusion with the mob or unfit.

accounts.label: Black Dispatch correspondents
accounts.gist: A Black posse followed a false police tip; the body, found hanging from an elm with two bullet wounds in the forehead and hands and feet tied, showed signs that only two or three men were at the scene.

accounts.label: Tulsa Star
accounts.gist: Chandler was seized while trying to get out of the doorway and no living witness could connect him with the killings; he was lynched largely because of his color.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP or UP dispatch, often under race-riot headlines such as the News Scimitar's 'Armed Negroes Are Reported En Route To Oklahoma City'.
The Daily Ardmoreite headlined Chandler a 'Black Bootlegger' while printing the governor's condemnation in full.
The Durant Weekly News mocked the killing with 'May Have Taken Him to Watermelon Feast' and a joke about a 'possum supper.
The Guthrie Daily Leader blamed Oklahoma County officers and doubted Chandler's guilt.
The Black Dispatch called it 'the most dastardly and hellish crime' in the state's history and accused the sheriff and jailer of guilty knowledge.
The Tulsa Star said he was lynched 'largely because of his color' but rebuked the Black men who armed themselves afterward.
Chicago and Cleveland papers ran short items: 'Lynched for Making Home Brew'; 'the lynchers go unmolested'.
